pr_title: Add REST API method to revoke role permissions
pr_body:
Adding `POST /roles/{role_name}/actions/revoke` method to revoke permissions assigned to a role.

Closes: #18714
pr_comments: In the linked issue it was discussed that `PATCH /roles/{role_name}` didn't work as expected and should've been documented. Completely aligned, I believe it should go through the deprecation now and probably be replaced with something like `POST /roles/{role_name}/actions` or `POST /roles/{role_name}/permissions` (if we decide that we can rename it to the latter). But for sure, it's a matter of a different PR.

issue_context.title: Make it possible to delete a permission from a role using the stable REST API
issue_context.body:
### Description

I'd like to be able to delete a permission from a role using the stable REST API.  Right now, when using the `PATCH` verb on the `/roles/{role_name}` endpoint, the actions and resources combo that gets added through the body is merged into the database, making it possible to add permissions but not delete them from what I can see.

I'd like to have the option to delete a permission from a role, which I don't believe is currently possible using `PATCH`.

### Use case/motivation

I want to be able to better modify Roles using the API.  Maybe as part of CI/CD I can set up the roles to my liking by using a script which calls the API, and can change roles.  Having more control over the Roles through the API would be a good feature for users of Airflow and useful specifically for my use-case involving the Astronomer platform.

### Related issues

_No response_

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

comments:
> the actions and resources combo that gets added through the body is merged into the database, making it possible to add permissions but not delete them from what I can see.

This feels like a bug to me. If `permissions` is provided, it should replace the entire permission list instead of merging the given permissions into the existing ones.
Might be just a problem with my misunderstanding of this endpoint, also see #18713 for my confusion 👀

Yeah the behavior that I'm seeing is that the permission list is being merged rather than replacing the entire thing.  This is corroborated by `security_manager.update_role` function call that is happening which is running a merge on the DB with the role.  You think that this is a bug @uranusjr ?  I'm thinking the same thing, but really don't know a ton about the nature of these `PATCH` endpoints to be able to make that kind of distinction.

REST API is only a guide line without hard rules, but `PATCH` generally means the user can submit a subset of fields, and the missing fields would be filled by existing values on the model. It is a natural variant to PUT, which _replaces_ all fields on the model with new values specified in the request.

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5789#section-2

> The difference between the PUT and PATCH requests is reflected in the way the server processes the enclosed entity to modify the resource identified by the Request-URI.  In a PUT request, the enclosed entity is considered to be a modified version of the resource stored on the origin server, and the client is requesting that the stored version be replaced.  With PATCH, however, the enclosed entity contains a set of instructions describing how a resource currently residing on the origin server should be modified to produce a new version.  The PATCH method affects the resource identified by the Request-URI, and it also MAY have side effects on other resources; i.e., new resources may be created, or existing ones modified, by the application of a PATCH.

Now it is entirely undefined whether sending a list in PATCH should mean merging the lists in the request and the existing object, or replacing the entire list on the existing object with the one in the request. But the merging behaviour does not really make common sense since it would make deleting entries impossible. So I'm inclined to think the current behaviour is wrong.
Maybe we make a new `PUT` endpoint that has the behavior that we expect?
We can, although the current PATCH behaviour is still somehow unintuitive and should at least be documented.
Heard that.  I'll make that a part of this PR that I started working on for this.

Hello, any news on this topic ? 
It's quite blocking if we want to set up a management logic outside the UI for the roles.
@erdrix - how about providing a PR to that one? This is the easiest way to do it and you can become one of the ~ 2000 contributors to Airlfow.
Especially if it is business-critical for you, it only seems reasonable to pay-back for the free software you get by contributing back this small feature.

I was investigating the possible cause of the problem.

I was confused because the name of the [patch_role](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/main/airflow/providers/fab/auth_manager/api_endpoints/role_and_permission_endpoint.py#L121-L151) function uses the PUT method in the decorator above, but the behavior is actually PATCH and not PUT, as this function calls the [bulk_sync_roles](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/main/airflow/providers/fab/auth_manager/security_manager/override.py#L1396-L1412) function which only adds the roles and to have the PUT behavior it should have [delete_role](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/main/airflow/providers/fab/auth_manager/security_manager/override.py#L1472-L1485) inside this function.

I don't have in-depth knowledge of Python development, so I could be saying something wrong, I'm just trying to help identify the possible cause and contribute in some way to this issue

review_comments:
It may be debatable if `409` or `404` or `204` should be returned if some of the passed permission pairs aren't assigned to the role.

For `409` vs `404`, I feel that we're dealing more with a conflicting state of the role object, rather than stating that some object isn't found. For non-existing actions or resources we're already returning `400` (aligned with the existing APIs). Also related to the topic: https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/issues/69

For `409` vs `204`, I think this is similar to the question "Should DELETE return 204 if the resource doesn't exist?" (https://stackoverflow.com/a/60695301). There may be an argument that the requester wants a particular state and  reaches that, so we're all good. That sounds fair and, to be honest, I haven't come up with a specific example, when it may be particularly bad, but still decided to stick to the current interface, which aligns with the UNIX `rm` and Python `list.remove` behaviour. Also if needed, it can be extended with a `force` flag to ignore the assigned permissions check.

Happy to discuss!

Personally my preference is between 404 and 204 actually; Conflict doesn’t seem like the right word for this and instead sound like the revocation failed due to the permission being needed by another resource.

> Conflict doesn’t seem like the right word for this

I would propose not to rely on the definition of the word itself, which is broad indeed, but more on the RFC guidance:

https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.409

> [15.5.10. ](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.5.10)[409 Conflict](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-409-conflict)
The 409 (Conflict) status code indicates that the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource. This code is used in situations where the user might be able to resolve the conflict and resubmit the request. The server SHOULD generate content that includes enough information for a user to recognize the source of the conflict.
>
> Conflicts are most likely to occur in response to a PUT request. For example, if versioning were being used and the representation being PUT included changes to a resource that conflict with those made by an earlier (third-party) request, the origin server might use a 409 response to indicate that it can't complete the request. In this case, the response representation would likely contain information useful for merging the differences based on the revision history. 

What we have here fits quite well, I suppose? Other than the method, which is `POST` instead of `PUT`, but I explained why in another thread.

I also look at this like if somebody had revoked the permissions I was going to revoke before me (e.g., race conditions), which resulted in a conflict between the states.

> and instead sound like the revocation failed due to the permission being needed by another resource.

That's absolutely fair interpretation as well! I'd just say that it doesn't cancel a validity for the above interpretation. A status may unwrap into multiple different subcases, the request may conflict with the resource state in different ways.

> the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource

But the reason the request cannot be completed is the target resource (the permission to revoke) does not exist. If that counts as a conflict, 404 won’t exist at all. IMO 404 is better if you this should emit an error.

I think if we look at a permission as the target resource here, then your reasoning makes perfect sense to me. I was rather looking at this more as changing a part of a role's state.

I'm happy to move to `404`, though wondering if you know anybody from the community, who may want to chime in? So that I don't need to migrate back and forth :)

Since in my current implementation I want to use `409` for a specific case (put some thoughts in another comment thread), which is different from the `AlreadyExists` case.

Generally I think `AlreadyExists` is a bit narrow for `409` and we may need a broader `Conflict` class at some point in the future anyway. The question is if we should just rename `AlreadyExists` into `Conflict` for the simplicity or maintain two classes for `409`, which also happens in some APIs, I believe, to differentiate between some cases under a broader HTTP code. Though if we want to maintain the both internally as well as in the REST API, then the work with `EXCEPTIONS_LINK_MAP` may slightly change, since its dict structure won't allow that.

Given that `AlreadyExists` actually already says _Conflict_ in the message, I’d say let’s just rename it (maybe add a line `AlreadyExists = Conflict` just in case, but even that’s not necessary IMO).

(Assuming we do want this new name, of course; that discussion is for the other thread.)

I'm not sure why this `if item` case is maintained.. I would love to be more opinionated about that, but don't want to break backward compatibility even for this weird case. To be stricter in my endpoint I would need to duplicate all the involved schemas marking the fields as `required`. 

And maybe I'm just missing a good reason, when it's needed.
Probably it still may be prone to race condition and require more isolation, but not sure how far we should go if we go this way :)

Actually it's not aligned with other implementations in this module (mostly borrowed from FAB, as far as I understand), which either return a bool flag or just suppress the exception. To be honest, I don't completely understand why it's the case. I'd stick to "throw early, catch late" (https://softwareengineering.stackexchange.com/questions/231057/exceptions-why-throw-early-why-catch-late), a complete suppressing may be quite confusing.
